title: Poisson Distribution
description: Modelling rare events with the Poisson distribution, calculating probabilities, and using its unique mean = variance property.

notes.heading: What is a Poisson Distribution?
notes.body:
The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that counts how many times an event occurs in a fixed interval of time or space.

It is perfect for rare, random events like emails arriving in an inbox, cars passing a speed camera, or flaws in a sheet of glass.

📌 Definition
A discrete random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution, written $X \sim \text{Po}(m)$, if:
• Occurrences are independent of each other
• Occurrences happen at a constant average rate $m$

There is no upper limit on how many times the event can occur.

🔑 Notation

$$X \sim \text{Po}(m)$$

$m =$ average rate of occurrences for the interval

💡 Worked Example
Jack uses $X \sim \text{Po}(6.25)$ to model the number of emails he receives during his one-hour lunch break.

  Step 1: State the two assumptions
    • Emails arrive independently (one email does not trigger another)
    • Emails arrive at a uniform average rate of $6.25$ per hour

  Step 2: Find the standard deviation
    For a Poisson distribution, $\text{Var}(X) = m$
    $\text{SD}(X) = \sqrt{m} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5$ emails

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Poisson is discrete — it counts whole occurrences only
• There is no fixed number of trials (unlike binomial)
• Events can theoretically keep happening forever
• The model works for time periods or spatial areas

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing Poisson with binomial. Binomial needs a fixed number of trials $n$ and a probability $p$. Poisson needs only a rate $m$ and has no maximum count.

illustration.caption: The Poisson distribution models rare, independent events occurring at a constant average rate. Its unique property is that the mean equals the variance, both equal to λ.

notes.heading: The Poisson Formula and Key Properties
notes.body:
The Poisson distribution has one of the simplest formulas in statistics, yet it carries remarkably powerful properties.

🔑 Probability Formula

$$P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-m} \cdot m^r}{r!}$$

for $r = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

  where:
    $e \approx 2.718$ (Euler's constant)
    $m =$ mean number of occurrences
    $r! = r \times (r - 1) \times \ldots \times 2 \times 1$, and $0! = 1$

🔑 Mean and Variance

$$E(X) = m$$
$$\text{Var}(X) = m$$
$$\text{SD}(X) = \sqrt{m}$$

  This mean = variance property is unique to the Poisson distribution.

🔑 Sum of Independent Poisson Variables

  If $X \sim \text{Po}(m)$ and $Y \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)$ are independent, then:

$$X + Y \sim \text{Po}(m + \lambda)$$

  This extends to any number of independent Poisson variables.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Using the Formula
For $X \sim \text{Po}(3)$, find $P(X = 2)$.

  Step 1: Substitute into the formula

$$P(X = 2) = \dfrac{e^{-3} \cdot 3^2}{2!}$$

  Step 2: Calculate each part
    $e^{-3} \approx 0.0498$
    $3^2 = 9$
    $2! = 2$

  Step 3: Combine

$$P(X = 2) = \dfrac{0.0498 \times 9}{2} \approx 0.224$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Sum Property
Cars pass a junction at an average rate of $5$ per minute. Buses pass independently at $2$ per minute. Find the distribution of total vehicles.

  Step 1: Define the variables
    $C \sim \text{Po}(5)$ for cars
    $B \sim \text{Po}(2)$ for buses

  Step 2: Apply the sum property

$$C + B \sim \text{Po}(5 + 2) = \text{Po}(7)$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Mean and variance are both equal to $m$ — always
• The distribution is right-skewed for small $m$, becoming more symmetric as $m$ grows
• You can add independent Poisson variables by adding their means
• If sample mean $\approx$ sample variance for discrete data, a Poisson model might fit

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that $0! = 1$. When calculating $P(X = 0)$, the formula becomes $P(X = 0) = \dfrac{e^{-m} \cdot m^0}{0!} = e^{-m}$. Students sometimes think $m^0 = 0$ or $0! = 0$.

notes.heading: Calculating Poisson Probabilities
notes.body:
Your GDC is the fastest way to find Poisson probabilities. Know which function to use and how to rewrite inequalities.

📌 GDC Functions
• Poisson PD (or Poisson Pdf) — finds $P(X = x)$ for a single value
• Poisson CD (or Poisson Cdf) — finds $P(a \leq X \leq b)$ or $P(X \leq x)$

🔑 Converting Inequalities for Your GDC

$$P(X < x) = P(X \leq x - 1)$$
$$P(X > x) = 1 - P(X \leq x)$$
$$P(X \geq x) = 1 - P(X \leq x - 1)$$
$$P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(X \leq b) - P(X \leq a - 1)$$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Single and Cumulative Values
Let $X \sim \text{Po}(4)$. Find $P(X \leq 2)$ and $P(X > 1)$.

  Part A: $P(X \leq 2)$
    Use Poisson CD with $x = 2$, $m = 4$
    $P(X \leq 2) \approx 0.238$

  Part B: $P(X > 1)$
    Rewrite: $P(X > 1) = 1 - P(X \leq 1)$
    Use Poisson CD with $x = 1$, $m = 4$
    $P(X \leq 1) \approx 0.0916$
    $P(X > 1) = 1 - 0.0916 = 0.908$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Range Probability
Let $X \sim \text{Po}(5)$. Find $P(2 \leq X \leq 4)$.

  Step 1: Rewrite using cumulative probabilities

$$P(2 \leq X \leq 4) = P(X \leq 4) - P(X \leq 1)$$

  Step 2: Use Poisson CD
    $P(X \leq 4) \approx 0.4405$
    $P(X \leq 1) \approx 0.0404$

  Step 3: Subtract

$$P(2 \leq X \leq 4) \approx 0.4405 - 0.0404 = 0.440$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $X$ must be a non-negative integer — no fractions or negatives
• Strict inequalities ($<$ and $>$) differ from weak ones ($\leq$ and $\geq$) by exactly $1$
• For ranges, always subtract the cumulative up to $(a - 1)$ from the cumulative up to $b$
• If your GDC only does $P(X \leq x)$, use the conversion identities above

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using $P(X < x) = P(X \leq x)$. For discrete distributions, $P(X < 5) = P(X \leq 4)$, not $P(X \leq 5)$. That one-integer difference is the most common source of lost marks.

notes.heading: Modelling with the Poisson Distribution
notes.body:
Setting up a Poisson model is about translating a real-world scenario into the correct random variable and mean rate.

📌 Steps to Build a Poisson Model
1. Identify what counts as a single occurrence
2. Determine the mean rate $m$ for the relevant interval
3. State your random variable clearly
4. Check that independence and constant-rate conditions hold

🔑 Scaling the Mean Rate

  $m$ scales linearly with time or space.

  If $12$ cars pass in $5$ minutes, then in $15$ minutes:

$$m = 12 \times \dfrac{15}{5} = 36$$

💡 Worked Example — Scaling and Modelling
A call centre receives $8$ calls in $30$ minutes on average.

  Step 1: Define the random variable for $15$ minutes
    Let $X$ be the number of calls in a $15$-minute period.

  Step 2: Scale the mean
    $15$ minutes is half of $30$ minutes.

$$m = 8 \times \dfrac{15}{30} = 4$$

  Step 3: State the distribution

$$X \sim \text{Po}(4)$$

  Step 4: Check conditions
    • Calls are independent
    • Calls arrive at a constant average rate
    The model is appropriate.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always write "Let $X$ be the number of ..." in exam answers
• Scale $m$ using proportion — double the time means double the mean
• The model also works for space (e.g. flaws per square metre)
• If events cluster or one triggers another, the model breaks down

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to scale the mean when the time period changes. If the question gives a rate for one interval but asks about another, you must adjust $m$ proportionally before calculating any probabilities.

notes.heading: Poisson Approximation to the Binomial
notes.body:
The binomial distribution can be hard to calculate when $n$ is very large. In some cases, a Poisson distribution gives an excellent approximation.

📌 Definition
If $X \sim B(n,p)$ with $n$ large, $p$ small, and $np$ moderate, then $X$ can be approximated by a Poisson distribution with mean $m = np$:
$$X \sim \text{Po}(np)$$
A common rule of thumb is $n \ge 20$ and $p \le 0.05$ (or $np \le 10$).

🔑 Why it works
When $n$ is large and $p$ is small, each trial is a rare event. The binomial formula simplifies toward the Poisson formula because $(1-p)^{n-r} \approx e^{-np}$.

💡 Worked Example
A factory produces light bulbs. The probability that a bulb is defective is $0.02$. In a batch of $100$ bulbs, find the approximate probability of exactly $3$ defectives.

  Step 1: Check conditions
    $n = 100$ is large, $p = 0.02$ is small, and $np = 2$ is moderate.

  Step 2: Choose the approximating distribution
    Let $X$ be the number of defectives. Then $X$ is approximately Poisson with $X \sim \text{Po}(2)$.

  Step 3: Calculate
$$P(X = 3) = \dfrac{e^{-2} \cdot 2^3}{3!} = \dfrac{e^{-2} \cdot 8}{6} \approx 0.180$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Use the approximation only when $n$ is large and $p$ is small
• Set the Poisson mean to $m = np$
• The approximation improves as $n \to \infty$ and $p \to 0$ with $np$ fixed
• It is an approximation, not an exact distribution

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the Poisson approximation when $p$ is not small or when $np$ is large. If $p$ is close to $0.5$, a normal approximation to the binomial is more appropriate.

notes.heading: Shape of the Poisson Distribution
notes.body:
The Poisson distribution is not symmetric; its shape depends entirely on the value of the mean $m$.

🔑 How it works
For small $m$, the distribution is strongly right-skewed, with the highest probabilities concentrated at $0$ or $1$. As $m$ increases, the distribution becomes more spread out and more symmetric, eventually resembling a bell shape.

💡 Worked Example
Compare $X \sim \text{Po}(1)$ and $Y \sim \text{Po}(8)$.

  For $X$:
    $P(X = 0) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368$ is the largest probability.
    The probabilities form a long tail to the right.

  For $Y$:
    Probabilities are centred around $8$ and the shape is much more symmetric.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Poisson is discrete and defined only for non-negative integers
• Small $m$ produces strong right skew
• Large $m$ produces an approximately symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
• There is no upper limit on the possible values of $X$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Treating the Poisson distribution as symmetric for small $m$. Intervals and tail probabilities must account for the skew.

✅ Check
If $m = 0.5$, would you expect many large values? No — most observations will be $0$ or $1$.

notes.heading: Choosing Between Binomial and Poisson Models
notes.body:
Both the binomial and Poisson distributions model counts, but they apply in different situations. Choosing the right model is often the first step to earning full marks.

📌 Definition
Use a binomial distribution when there is a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Use a Poisson distribution when events occur independently at a constant average rate over time or space, with no fixed upper limit.

🔑 Key Concept
Ask yourself: "Is there a maximum possible number of occurrences?"

  • If yes, the binomial distribution is usually appropriate.
  • If no, the Poisson distribution is usually appropriate.

💡 Worked Example
Scenario A: Count the number of sixes in $20$ rolls of a fair die.
  There is a fixed number of trials ($n = 20$).
  Model: $X \sim B(20, \dfrac{1}{6})$.

Scenario B: Count the number of sixes rolled during a $5$-minute period.
  There is no fixed number of rolls.
  Model: $Y \sim \text{Po}(m)$, where $m$ is the average rate of sixes per $5$ minutes.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Binomial: fixed $n$, independence, constant success probability $p$
• Poisson: constant average rate, independence, no upper bound
• Some problems can be modelled either way when the Poisson approximates the binomial
• Always state your random variable and its parameters in exam answers

⚠️ Common Mistake
Choosing a Poisson model just because the events are rare. Always check whether there is a fixed number of trials; if there is, binomial is the natural choice.

flashcards.term: When to use a Poisson model
flashcards.definition: Use Poisson when events are independent, occur at a constant average rate, and have no fixed upper limit.
flashcards.example: Counting calls to a help desk in a one-hour period.

flashcards.definition: For discrete $X$, $P(X < x) = P(X \le x - 1)$, $P(X > x) = 1 - P(X \le x)$, and $P(X \ge x) = 1 - P(X \le x - 1)$.

questions.stem: For $X \sim \text{Po}(2.5)$, what is $P(X = 3)$ to 3 significant figures?
A discrete random variable has mean $6$ and variance $6$. Which distribution might model it?
questions.explanation: The Poisson distribution is the only one where mean = variance = $m$. $B(12, 0.5)$ has mean $6$ but variance $3$. $N(6, 6)$ is continuous, not discrete.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Po}(2)$ and $Y \sim \text{Po}(5)$ are independent. What is the distribution of $X + Y$?
questions.explanation: The sum of independent Poisson variables is also Poisson with mean equal to the sum of the individual means: $2 + 5 = 7$.

questions.stem: On average, a call centre receives $8$ calls in $30$ minutes. Using a Poisson model, what is the mean number of calls in a $15$-minute period?
questions.explanation: The mean scales proportionally with time. $15$ minutes is half of $30$ minutes, so $m = 8/2 = 4$.
$P(2 \leq X \leq 4) = P(X \leq 4) - P(X \leq 1)$. Using Poisson CD: $P(X \leq 4) \approx 0.4405$ and $P(X \leq 1) \approx 0.0404$. Difference $\approx 0.440$.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to use a Poisson distribution?
choices: Events occur at a constant average rate
There is a fixed maximum number of trials
The mean and variance are approximately equal
questions.explanation: Poisson does NOT require a fixed number of trials — that is a feature of the binomial distribution. Poisson events can theoretically occur without limit.

questions.stem: $X \sim \text{Po}(6)$. What is the standard deviation of $X$?
questions.explanation: For $X \sim \text{Po}(m)$, $\text{Var}(X) = m$, so $\text{SD}(X) = \sqrt{m} = \sqrt{6}$. Note that $2.45$ is $\sqrt{6}$ rounded, but $\sqrt{6}$ is the exact answer.

questions.stem: A machine produces defective items with probability $0.03$. In a batch of $200$ items, which Poisson distribution approximates the number of defectives?
questions.explanation: For a Poisson approximation to the binomial, use $m = np = 200 \times 0.03 = 6$.

questions.stem: For which value of $m$ is the Poisson distribution most strongly right-skewed?
questions.explanation: The Poisson distribution is most skewed when the mean is small; larger means produce a more symmetric shape.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the variance of a Poisson distribution?
choices: Variance is greater than the mean
Variance is less than the mean
Variance equals the square of the mean
questions.explanation: For $X \sim \text{Po}(m)$, both the expected value and the variance equal $m$.

questions.stem: A call centre receives an average of $3$ calls every $10$ minutes. Using a Poisson model, what is the mean number of calls in a $40$-minute period?
questions.explanation: The mean scales linearly with time: $m = 3 \times \dfrac{40}{10} = 12$.
